decisions.quote: MacKuen, Erikson, and Stimson (1989, 1992) argue that the aggregate distribution of party identification, or macropartisanship, shifts significantly over short periods in response to changes in presidential popularity and consumer sentiment. Their results are based on a subset of Gallup surveys available from 1953 to 1988 and only those CBS/New York Timessurveys conducted during the Reagan administration. We replicate this analysis using a more extensive inventory of Gallup and CBS/New York Timesdata and find considerably less evidence of partisan fluctuation. The amount of partisan change caused by short-term movements in consumer sentiment and presidential popularity is found to be two to three times smaller than initially reported by MacKuen et al. (1989).
decisions.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies MacKuen, Erikson, and Stimson (1989) on macropartisanship (1953-1988 survey data) as the replicated analysis, matching the shipped original (10.2307/1961661) and blind target 0; the absence of a reference list in the abstract-only source does not establish an error in the shipped DOI or title.

decisions.quote: We replicate this analysis using a more extensive inventory of Gallup and CBS/New York Timesdata and find considerably less evidence of partisan fluctuation. The amount of partisan change caused by short-term movements in consumer sentiment and presidential popularity is found to be two to three times smaller than initially reported by MacKuen et al. (1989). Our results indicate that macropartisanship adjusts to short-term shocks in a limited and gradual fashion, consistent with traditional views of partisan realignment.
decisions.reason: Contrary to MacKuen et al.'s (1989) claim that macropartisanship shifts significantly over short periods, the authors frame their replication as a critique that finds considerably less partisan fluctuation and supports traditional views of limited, gradual adjustment, confirming the shipped 'failed' outcome.
